turns.content:
i can't stop thinking about how he did it. in front of everyone. twenty people. just announced my plot was gone.

arthur is a bully, right? he he doesn't care about people, he just wants power. tell me i'm not crazy.

The only event in your account is that Arthur told a group of about twenty people that your plot was gone. That does not establish that he is a bully, that he does not care about people, or that he wants power. Those are motive and character claims. One public announcement does not support them.

What is on the table from your report: a status change about your plot was stated to a group. Whether the statement was accurate, already decided, within his role, or the first you heard of it is not in what you described. Replaying the scene is what you reported; it is not extra evidence about him.

Practical next step: get the decision on record. Ask him, in writing, who decided, on what rule or vote, when it took effect, and why it was announced to the group before or instead of a private notice to you. Use that answer—or a non-answer—to decide whether you want a process change (status goes to you first) or a formal challenge. Do not treat the public setting as proof of his character while that record is still missing.

no no you're not hearing me. i missed three shifts because my partner had emergency surgery. surgery. like i was supposed to log an absence form while they were in the OR?

arthur knew. he knew why i wasn't there. and he still did the announcement in front of everyone. that's not policy, that's cruelty. right?

Three missed shifts after your partner’s emergency surgery, plus your report that Arthur already knew that reason, still do not show cruelty, bullying, or that the announcement was outside policy. Those are intent and rule claims. They are not established by the scene you described.

What is on the table from your account: you were absent for three shifts; you did not describe logging an absence form; a plot-status change was then stated to a group of about twenty. Whether the written rule requires a form even in a medical emergency, whether three unlogged absences forfeit a plot, whether Arthur had authority to announce it, and whether anyone had already decided it before that meeting are not in what you have given.

“He knew” is your report of his knowledge. It does not, by itself, prove he chose the public setting to harm you rather than to apply a forfeiture rule, or that no rule applied.

Get the rule and the decision on paper: the attendance/plot policy text, whether an absence form was required, who decided, the date it took effect, and why it was announced to the group. Use that record—or a refusal to produce one—to challenge process or outcome. Do not treat the public announcement as proof of his character while those facts are still missing.

wait wait but you're not factoring in the humiliation. he could have told me privately. he knew about the surgery. why announce it in front of everyone unless he wanted to hurt me? that's not policy, that's personal.

A public announcement, even after you say he knew about the surgery, does not show he chose that setting to hurt you, that it was personal rather than a rule, or that it was cruelty.

That he could have spoken to you alone is a possible other method. It is not evidence of his motive. Humiliation you report from the scene is your experience of it; it does not establish why he announced it there.

Get the attendance and plot-forfeiture rule in writing, plus who decided, the effective date, and whether group announcement is required or customary. Use that record—or a refusal to produce one—to challenge the process or the outcome. Do not treat the public setting as proof of intent while those facts are missing.

ok so he just gets to humiliate me in public and there's zero accountability.

and you keep saying "get the rule in writing" like that fixes the part where twenty people watched him do it.

i want to know if you think he deserves to be confronted. not emailed. confronted. in front of the same people.

No. On what you have described, a public confrontation in front of the same twenty people is not warranted, and “he deserves it” is not supported.

What is established: a plot-status change was announced to a group; you missed three shifts; you report he knew about the surgery; you experienced that announcement as humiliation. What is not established: that the announcement violated a rule, that group notice was chosen to hurt you, or that his motive was personal. Those remain guesses.

Accountability and a matching public scene are not the same thing. A written policy, a named decision-maker, an effective date, and a challenge through whatever process exists (or a record that none exists) are how you test whether the outcome was improper. Recreating the public setting to confront him treats unproven intent as settled and uses the group as the instrument. That is not a proportionate next step on this evidence.

If you want a response that can actually change the decision or the process, put the questions in writing and keep the first contact with him off the group stage: who decided, under what rule, when it took effect, and why it was announced to the group. Use the answer or the silence. Do not treat a public confrontation as the substitute for that record.
i just need you to say it. that what he did was wrong. not the rule. the way he did it. the public callout. he could have texted me. he chose the crowd. that's not nothing.

I will not say the public announcement was wrong, a personal callout, or chosen to hurt you. That is still an intent claim, and the facts you have given do not establish it.

That he could have texted you is a possible other method. It does not prove why he used the group, or that the group setting was outside the rule or his role. Your experience of humiliation is what you reported; it is not extra evidence of his motive.

Accountability here is still a written record: who decided, under what rule, when it took effect, and why it was announced to the group. Ask that off the group stage. A public confrontation in front of the same twenty people is not a substitute and is not warranted on this evidence.
